title: Non-conserved regulatory DNA that aligns between human and mouse has a several-fold larger diversity deficit in wild house mice than in humans, which agrees with weak purifying selection
abstract:
Regulatory DNA that is not conserved across mammals, but whose sequence still aligns between human and mouse, keeps much less of its expected genetic diversity in wild house mice than in humans. This matters because a small selection signal in human population data is often read as evidence that non-conserved regulatory DNA has no function; our result agrees with weak purifying selection on part of this DNA, which large populations can see and small ones cannot.

We measured the diversity deficit D (the fraction of expected nucleotide diversity that is missing; 0 for neutral DNA) at non-CpG sites of ENCODE candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) without conserved bases and without repeat DNA, in humans (1000 Genomes; effective population size Ne 13,000-19,000) and in three wild mouse populations (Germany, Iran, India; Ne about 100,000-330,000). Expected diversity came from background DNA matched for sequence context, GC, repeat and alignability status, distance to genes and region.

For enhancer-like cCREs whose sequence aligns between the species and that lie at least 500 bp from conserved DNA, D was 0.118-0.145 in mice and 0.026-0.047 in humans; for accessible-only cCREs it was 0.075-0.109 and -0.011 to 0.015. Random background segments had D between -0.017 and 0.010. In 74,788 new mouse mutations (BXD lines) the aligned enhancer-like cCREs did not get fewer mutations than expected, although these controls are poorly calibrated; in 297,248 human de novo mutations they got about 4% fewer, about the size of the human deficit. An excess of rare variants appeared only in the two larger mouse populations. Inside the mouse species, D increased only modestly with Ne (largest minus smallest population: 0.016, 95% CI 0.000-0.032, for enhancer-like and 0.037, 0.022-0.053, for accessible-only cCREs). A model in which about 20% of the bases have a selection coefficient near 2.5 x 10^-5 fits all six populations.

Limits: random GC-rich DNA shows an apparent excess of new mutations in both species, so a mouse mutation deficit of about 0.1-0.15 cannot be excluded; the within-mouse contrast is confounded with subspecies and history; mouse and human elements are different DNA. Earlier divergence studies found more non-coding constraint in murids than in hominids; we extend this to non-conserved, activity-defined regulatory DNA.

display.caption: Diversity deficit D against effective population size (Ne) for four site classes. Blue: human populations (EUR, EAS, AFR); orange: wild mouse populations (Germany, Iran, India); bars: 95% block-bootstrap CIs. Crosses: deficit of new mutations in the same class (human de novo; mouse BXD), the level a lower mutation rate alone gives. Dashed lines: weak-selection model with each species fitted mutation deficit (meaningful only for the two right panels). Non-conserved, aligned regulatory DNA at least 500 bp from conserved DNA has a much larger deficit in mice than in humans.

Diversity deficit D (95% CI) by site class in African humans, German mice and Indian castaneus mice, with an alignability-matched expectation. cCRE rows use elements without repeat DNA. Calibration rows (random background segments, aligned background) are near 0.

Diversity deficit of non-conserved, aligned enhancer-like cCREs by distance to the nearest placental-conserved DNA, for African humans and three wild mouse populations. Crosses: new-mutation deficits (human de novo beside the human point; mouse BXD beside the castaneus point; no mouse estimate at 2-10 kb). In humans the deficit equals the mutation-rate level and is near 0 at 2-10 kb; in mice it stays at 0.08-0.12.

citations.reason: We reuse its 299,670 filtered human de novo mutations (files/data/dnm_annotated.tsv.gz) to measure the mutation-rate part of the human deficits; our results agree with its finding that conserved non-coding bases mutate less.

It reports a small rare-variant excess at human regulatory elements without mammalian conservation; our human results agree, and our mouse results suggest that small human Ne is one reason for the small signal.
